clue.text: Laying hands on a footballer or restraining yourself

definitions.meaning: grabbing hold of a defender, a full back or half back in football
checking an impulse, keeping oneself in reserve

explanation.definitionFit: A full back is a defender, so gripping one is the phrase taken literally; the idiom also means showing restraint or reluctance.

clue.text: Duck rise in panic from tree by the water

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: panic throws things into disorder, so the letters of rise are jumbled

explanation.surface: A duck takes fright and flies up from a waterside tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the bird taking off, but it is cricket's score of zero; the tree is the basket willow.
explanation.definitionFit: The willow used for basketry is a tree that typically grows on riverbanks.

clue.text: However, a spider did not make Bruce do it

definitions.text: However, a spider did not make Bruce do it

parts.words: However, a spider did not make Bruce do it
parts.note: legend says Robert the Bruce, hiding in a cave after defeats, watched a spider keep trying to spin its web and was inspired not to give up hope

explanation.surface: A nod to the legend of Robert the Bruce and the persistent spider.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert the Bruce was a medieval King of Scotland; the spider story is a well-known Scottish legend about perseverance.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing all hope is what the spider supposedly stopped the defeated king from doing.

clue.text: Cite functioning upset in one's mind

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the combined letters are rearranged

parts.note: a machine that is functioning is on

explanation.surface: Someone quotes a working example that troubles them mentally.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a philosophical adjective for things of the intellect, existing in thought.

clue.text: Graduate erring rather too much

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate's degree
someone erring morally is sinful

explanation.surface: A university graduate who has strayed into excess.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a bowlful of something unwelcome is an excess: 'I've had a bellyful of it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial phrase 'a bowlful of' means more than enough, an excessive amount.

clue.text: Takes a turn on deck

parts.note: read as a sailor taking a turn of duty, but it describes a ship's machine that is itself rotated on the deck to haul a rope

explanation.surface: A sailor does a stint of duty up top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes a turn' suggests someone's shift; the thing meant is turned by sailors pushing bars to wind in cable.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's vertical winch is rotated on deck to wind an anchor cable.

clue.text: Military action when the sales doors open?

definitions.meaning: a retaliatory attack by troops answering an enemy's attack
playfully, the stampede of shoppers to the shop counters when a sale begins

explanation.definitionFit: A retaliatory assault is the military sense; the playful sense is bargain hunters rushing the shop counters.

clue.text: Drawsvehicles up in'a race to pole

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Drawsvehicles up in'a race to pole' for ATTRACTS: A + TT (race) + S (pole) leaves RACT, which no reversal of a vehicles word (CARTS gives STRAC) supplies; no sound parse found.
annotationWithheld.clue: Drawsvehicles up in'a race to pole

clue.text: Meals on wheels supplied by them

definitions.text: Meals on wheels supplied by them

indicators.note: supplied is read as made supple, bent into new shape, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bulk traders are the people who provide food delivered to the housebound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supplied' rearranges all thirteen letters of MEALS ON WHEELS; the whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Traders selling in bulk to shops supply goods, here pictured as supplying meals.

clue.text: Oddly moist drops

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, so the letters of moist are rearranged

explanation.surface: Damp falls from something in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like a call for alternate letters, but here it rearranges MOIST.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop something from a list is to leave it out, a synonym.

clue.text: Liked by batsmen rather than bowlers

definitions.text: Liked by batsmen rather than bowlers

parts.words: Liked by batsmen rather than bowlers
parts.note: a cricket surface that gives the bowler no help, so batting is comfortable

explanation.surface: A cricket preference that batters share and bowlers dislike.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the pitch is the strip of turf between the wickets; a flat, true one favours batsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: A docile, true cricket strip makes scoring runs straightforward for the batting side.

clue.text: Managed to withdraw from share account

indicators.note: withdraw means draw back, so the word for managed is turned backwards

parts.note: to manage a business is to run it, past tense ran
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: Someone managed to take money out of a joint savings account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to withdraw' turns RAN back to NAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An account of events is a telling or storytelling, a synonym.

clue.text: Mountainous area too much for a novice.

parts.note: a tyro is a beginner
L is a learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A hilly region is too challenging for a beginner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'too much' hints at 'two much': the novice is given twice, TYRO then L. L-plates mark British learner drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: This Alpine region of Austria and Italy is famous for its mountains.

clue.text: Repeat directions to the centre

parts.note: E and N, east and north, are compass directions
the core of something is its centre

explanation.surface: Instructions on how to reach the middle are given again.
explanation.definitionFit: A performance given again at the audience's call is a repeat.

clue.text: Many a police force bribe gets cross

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number
RUC, the Royal Ulster Constabulary, was Northern Ireland's police force
a means one, the Roman numeral I
to fix something is to rig it with a bribe

explanation.surface: Many a corrupt police officer leaves someone angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like 'angry', but it defines a cross bearing Christ's figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross bearing the figure of Christ is a religious emblem.

clue.text: Confronts vessel in places where. the fire is concentrated

definitions.text: places where. the fire is concentrated

indicators.note: in places the word for vessel inside the word for confronts

parts.note: to confront is to face
an urn is a vase-like vessel

explanation.surface: Someone stands up to a ship where the firefighting is heaviest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship, but it is an urn.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial hearths are enclosures in which intense heat is kept up.

clue.text: Scottish charm?

parts.note: a lucky charm, and also the title of a novel by Sir Walter Scott, so 'Scottish' means by Scott

explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a charm, and it is also a Walter Scott novel title.

clue.text: There must be reason behind this' method of road construction

parts.note: a cause is a reason
a way of doing something is a method

explanation.surface: A grumble that a building technique must have a justification.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised road built across wet ground is a kind of roadway construction.

clue.text: Carried on shoulder of English boy and Parisian

parts.note: Paul is a boy's name
a Parisian says et for and

explanation.surface: An English lad and a French one carried something on their shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: This ornamental shoulder piece on a uniform is worn on the shoulder.

clue.text: May contain or displace water

parts.note: a jug holds water inside it, while a ship pushes water aside as it floats

explanation.surface: Something that might hold water or push it aside.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a container for liquids and a ship, which displaces water.

clue.text: He puts the champion out by one point

definitions.text: He puts the champion out by one point

parts.note: E, east, is one point of the compass
a victor is a champion

explanation.surface: A challenger beats the title holder by a single point.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes someone turning a person out of a home.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who expels a tenant from a property throws them out.

clue.text: Stable and attics converted

indicators.note: converted means changed into a new form, so the letters of attics are rearranged

explanation.surface: A horse's stable and loft rooms turned into homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like a building for horses beside the attics; it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Unchanging and steady describes something at rest, not moving.

clue.text: She gives Ian change, with thanks

indicators.note: to change a name is to alter it, so the letters of Ian are rearranged

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: A woman gives Ian his change and says thank you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' looks like coins handed over; it rearranges IAN into ANI. TA is British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so a female person, the she of the clue.

clue.text: Arouses interest with clandestine love affairs

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means fascinates; the plural noun means secret plots, including illicit romances.

clue.text: Combine it within French article

indicators.note: within places the word it inside the article

parts.note: une is the French indefinite article, feminine

explanation.surface: An item is merged into a piece in French.
explanation.definitionFit: To join together or merge things is to combine them.

clue.text: Bird showing remorse having injured then eaten mole

indicators.note: something eaten goes inside, so the word for remorse surrounds the rest

parts.note: guilt is a feeling of remorse

indicators.note: injured means hurt and damaged, so the letters of mole are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird feels remorse after injuring and eating a mole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having ... eaten' makes remorse the container; 'injured' scrambles the small animal, and 'then' only orders the two steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A seabird of the auk family that nests on cliffs.

clue.text: Beginning of the ceremony is meaningless

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, here of the

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony

explanation.surface: The opening of the ritual is empty of meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark worn out by overuse is hackneyed, carrying little real meaning.

clue.text: Bird dropping a twisted lock in fishpond

indicators.note: in puts the twisted lock and its article inside the fishpond

parts.note: a stew is an old word for a fishpond
one means a single, as a does
a curl is a twisted lock of hair

explanation.surface: A bird drops a corkscrew lock of hair into a fishpond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird dropping' is the misleading picture; 'dropping' is only a link. STEW meaning fishpond is an old word.
explanation.definitionFit: A wading bird of open stony country, also called the thick-knee.
